newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans lead grains higher, coffee also firm.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans lead grains higher, coffee also firm.

text.p: Soybean prices ended with sharp gains on Wednesday for a second consecutive day on talk that prices had fallen enough in recent weeks to attract fresh demand from overseas buyers.
Soybeans for July delivery at the Chicago Board of Trade closed up 21 cents a bushel at $7.89.

"That selloff last week caught the Brazilian FOB basis (export price) going in the other direction and put us into favorable price comparisons with Brazil," said Bob Lekberg, an analyst with Goldenberg-Hehmeyer. "That uncovered some new business."
Exporters said they could not confirm any deals, but there was widespread talk that two cargoes of soybeans were sold out of the Great Lakes to Europe this week.

Asian traders also said Chinese companies have been buying significant quantities of U.S. soybeans since early July when prices collapsed amid growing signs that the United States would harvest a record crop this fall.
Rumors of Chinese buying pushed soybean meal up sharply, with August meal closing up the daily allowable trading limit of $10 per ton at $243.80.
Corn prices rose as talk began to circulate about dry weather in some parts of the Midwest. Corn for July delivery closed up 6-1/2 cents a bushel at $2.49-3/4.

"Starting next week (and) on into August we'll be pollinating, and the weather is looking a little more uncertain," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Des Moines, Iowa. "We don't have much risk premium in corn."

Wheat prices rose on talk that Egypt, one of the largest buyers of U.S. wheat, might surprise the market and tender soon for wheat. Rains also slowed the harvest of winter wheat in some areas, easing pressure from hedge sales of futures by grain elevators buying cash wheat.
July wheat closed up 9-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.25-3/4.
"We had some harvest interruptions and then the talk of Egypt coming in," Lekberg said. "They have not issued a tender yet, but there is widespread belief that they will."

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures posted strong gains for a second day following a stunning cut in an Agriculture Department official's coffee crop estimate for Brazil, the top world producer.
Coffee for September delivery closed at 197.00 cents a pound, up 5.50 cents.

On Tuesday a report from the USDA's agricultural attache in Brazil put that country's current harvest at 24 million 132-pound bags, down sharply from the department's official estimate of 28 million bags published last month.

After the close on Wednesday, the department said it had confidence in its 28 million bag estimate and the lower estimate by a U.S. agricultural attache did not take into account all factors influencing the crop.
"We stand by our numbers and the integrity of our system," said Ed Cissel, director of production estimates and crop assessment for the USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended lower after weekly oil industry data showed substantial supplies and Iraq took another step toward resuming oil sales under a deal with the United Nations.

Crude oil for August delivery closed 27 cents a barrel lower at $19.46. August heating oil ended 0.35 cent a gallon lower at 52.65 cents and August gasoline ended 0.69 cent a gallon lower at 58.23 cents.

"Oil supplies are plentiful, and there is certainly more than enough gasoline supply to meet demand this summer. The report was bearish," said James Cordier, a trader with Allendale Inc, said of the weekly oil inventory released by the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday evening.

For the week ended July 4, U.S. crude oil stocks rose 4.7 million barrels when traders had been expecting a decline of 2 to 3 million barrels. Imports shot up to a hefty 8.96 million barrels per day from 8.51 million the week before.
In Baghdad, Iraqi officials gave the U.N. coordinator a preliminary draft of an aid distribution plan.
Staffan de Mistura, the U.N. coordinator, said some more work and further meetings were needed before the plan could be passed to the U.N. secretary-general for approval.

In May, the U.N. allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil for a second six-month period to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods. But oil sales have been held up pending completion of the distribution plan.
